summary: Upgrade and rollback: journal, snapshot, health gate, coordinator, side-by-side installs, and startup recovery wired into the daemon so the mechanism is used rather than merely present. Ordering is the design — snapshot, journal, migrate, gate, commit — with the point of no return last, because an upgrade that fails halfway leaves a store no binary can read. The 60s gate budget is ENFORCED, keeping the slow replay check asynchronous (P1-PERF: 50k-edge replay vs a 15-minute RTO); a gate that only documented its budget would pass it. THREE DEFECTS FOUND: rollback derived the store path from the snapshot's filename and passed only because the fixture put both in one folder; the atomic replace was not atomic because File.ReadAllText does not share delete, so a concurrent reader made the WRITER throw on Windows; and even after that fix a delete-pending file needs a bounded retry. TWO TESTS PROVED NOTHING until mutation said so — the enum-naming test asserted a round-tripped value, which numeric enums also satisfy, and nothing distinguished atomic replacement from an in-place write. Pruning protects the current build explicitly because after a rollback the current version is an older one. 13/13 mutations caught. 454 tests (+36), four gates clean. Health gate CONTENTS for a real schema migration are not built — the store has no migration chain yet — stated rather than faked.

prompt: do your best next action
summary: The first WRITE crosses the boundary: scope refresh. Started-and-polled rather than awaited on the wire, because a scope has a 60s budget and the lane serves one request at a time per connection — the control lane carries commands, and a command that starts long work returns once it is started. The command id is the idempotency key and this is where it first matters across processes; deduplication has two guards and only the concurrent one (TryAdd) is load-bearing, which a mutation run proved by disabling it with nothing failing. Job records are bounded because they are keyed by a caller-chosen id; a running job is never evicted. An incomplete extraction is a failure, not a refresh of zero. Reads and writes are separate seams. TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY MUTATION: announcements were not marshalled to the UI thread, so a re-index reporting its outcome from background work would throw exactly when telling the user something (fixed in WorkbenchAnnouncer, which owns the control); and RecordingAnnouncer was not thread-safe. The existing SC 2.5.7 catalog conformance test caught my palette entry having no handler. 9/9 mutations caught. 479 tests (+16), four gates clean. PROMPT DISPATCH IS BLOCKED ON A DIVERGENCE, NOT EFFORT: the design puts terminals in the daemon ('a crashed daemon must not leave agent CLIs running headless') and TerminalSurface creates them in the shell — recorded rather than half-crossed.
goal: Move the first write across the daemon boundary — scope refresh — so a daemon-backed workspace can be told to index
done_when: A shell re-indexes a scope over the pipe, idempotently, with a keyboard-reachable trigger; gates clean; committed

Renamed them and added a control that fails when one escapes; registered DC-018 (a guard that watches by name, and a name that moved). The terminal probe also lied twice before it was fixed: the seed must arrive before any absence is asserted, and the first run could not read workspace.db because SQLite held it open, so the store — the most important file — was never scanned while the probe reported success. Five steps. The first one measured, and the measurement withdrew my own proposal.

**Readiness.** I had written that one measurement would turn agent dispatch from always-refused into
working. It does not. A new observe-agent instrument captured what Claude Code actually draws:
the trust gate appears even in this repository's own directory; the chevron in the output is the
selection cursor of that dialog sitting on "No, exit"; and the screen is a TUI drawn with absolute
cursor addressing, so a tail-anchored regex over the byte stream asks where the cursor went last
rather than what the screen says. A looser marker — the obvious repair — would report READY at the
most dangerous possible moment. The built-in marker is left exactly as it is, the captured bytes are
a committed fixture, and the negative control was observed failing on a loosened pattern before being
accepted. Screen-buffer readiness is recorded as the next real step.

first. The migration chain's placeholder — a worked example describing a rename the product never
performed — was replaced by the real v1→v2 step, so the joins pane reaches users who already have a
saved layout; the example moved into the test that documents it. depends_on is consumed as a Verified
join. And DC-021 has an automated control: verify-fixture-derivation.py, which found two live cases
the hour it was written, one of them a day old and written by the same hand that registered the class.

summary:
Five steps. The third one found a defect in the second-to-last turn's work.

**A screen model.** ScreenBuffer is a small VT interpreter — cursor movement, erasure, text, nothing
else. Readiness now matches the rendered screen anchored to the last drawn line, because the earlier
measurement showed an agent's last bytes are wherever the cursor went rather than what the user sees.
The built-in markers are anchored at both ends and remain explicitly unverified against a ready agent.

**The trust gate is a state.** NeedsAttention, searched across the whole screen, outranking readiness,
announced once per transition rather than per repaint. Before this the shell refused and said nothing,
which is indistinguishable from a broken pane (DC-011).

**The joins, on a real repository — and DC-022.** The first run over TheTerrace reported 7,426
verified joins, each carrying "declared in the resource's dependsOn", in a repository containing no
Bicep and no dependsOn at all. depends_on is the C# extractor's predicate for type dependencies; the
join qualified on the PREDICATE rather than the kind of thing it was on, and its basis was a fixed
string that could never disagree with the evidence. It failed in the flattering direction — the
largest Verified count the pane had ever shown. Fixed, pinned by two tests, registered. After the fix:
0 verified, 59 inferred, which is the correct answer for that repository.

The contexts pane in the same run is usable, and names Operations as the boundary worth examining.
360 of 474 uncovered symbols are tests — the namespace grouping turned a number that reads as a gap
into a line that reads as correct.

**Two controls widened.** The fixture-derivation gate now watches command ids (29 identifiers,
observed firing on a planted literal), and the migration chain has both an end-to-end test and one
asserting the steps join up — which fails the moment a version is bumped without a migration.

ongoing builds could not disturb it.

built": AiDe.App.CanvasProbe was never a ProjectReference of the test project, so it had been built
once by a full-solution build and every run since had exercised that stale executable. Rebuilt from
current source it failed for real — the canvas page carried a JavaScript syntax error that broke the

keeps passing because it runs a stale build of the thing it tests.

Running the panes over TheTerrace found two more. hosted_on matched the whole Microsoft.Sql/* family
and produced a Cartesian product — 64 tables x 3 resources = 192 edges, each claiming to be the only
literally-named SQL resource, of which there were three. And the context-coverage denominator counted
Bicep parameters, so the map was blamed for artifacts it was never about.

A defect in the spike itself produced a confidently wrong write-up before that: extractors passed
positionally put BicepExtractor in the fallback slot, so every bicep scope was routed to the schema
extractor and failed, and the write-up concluded the repository had no Bicep. It has two templates
and 24 resources. Fixed with named arguments and corrected in the record.

The readiness watcher now uses the same TerminalScreen and VtParser the pane renders with; the
ScreenBuffer written last turn was a duplicate of a screen model this repository already had, and was
deleted.

AppDbContext. Operations is not a boundary that failed; the map counts shared persistence as domain
coupling.

summary:
Chose work on the core side of the line, and wrote the line down first.

The contract (docs/collaboration/session-contracts.md, status: proposed) states the seam in one
sentence — Core produces view models, Design renders them — lists file ownership rather than
describing it, names the eight contract types and the two invariants neither session may break
alone, and gives the three-step protocol for changing any of them. Section 6 lists what it does NOT
settle, because writing one session's preference down as settled is how a proposal becomes a fait
accompli. Three render requests are recorded in it rather than made in conversation.

Then two core defects.

The daemon composed only the C# extractor and the fixture adapter, so the running application could
not see infrastructure or schema — while a spike composed all four and reported joins the product had
no way to show. One composition now, WorkspaceExtractors.Default(), used by both, with named
arguments and a test that reads the routing decision rather than trusting parameter order. Observed
failing on the exact mis-ordering that caused the original wrong conclusion: expected "bicep", actual
"schema".

And every number both panes show was computed from a bounded read — 20,000 matches, 4,000 nodes, 60
neighbours each — that never said so. On the repositories measured the caps are slack, and nothing in
the output would change if they were not: the counts would just be smaller and still presented as
facts. EvidenceRead reports what the read did not see, both causes separately because their fixes
point in opposite directions, and a node at exactly the limit counts as truncated.

summary:
Four core steps, and they uncovered four more defects than they were aimed at.

Proving the daemon's extraction across the pipe failed first against a STALE Release daemon —
LocateDaemon preferred Release if the folder existed rather than following the configuration the
tests were built in. DC-023 in the harness. With that fixed the daemon does return infrastructure
evidence, asserted against the provenance extractor id rather than a predicate name.

Raising the caps found the real one: ProjectionService.Find borrowed MaxNeighborsCeiling, so the
workbench asked for 20,000 matches and received 50. The context and join panes have been computing
crossing counts, join counts and coverage from roughly three percent of a real workspace and
presenting it as the answer — while the spike read the store directly and showed everything. On
TheTerrace the panes now see 2,164 nodes instead of 50. The shell also invented its own total instead
of reading ResultBounds.OmittedNodes, and asked for 60 neighbours against a ceiling of 50, so the
truncation warning could never fire. It fires on 26 nodes now.

Incremental re-index takes TheTerrace from 4.3s to 0.1s, with reuse counted separately because "7 of
7 indexed" would be a true sentence about a run that read nothing. Testing it across a reopen found
that THE SECOND INDEX OF ANY WORKSPACE AFTER A RESTART FAILED — the generation counter started at
zero on every open while the store did not. The daemon opens the store fresh every start; nothing had
ever indexed twice across a reopen.

A third repository made the DC-022 collision live rather than hypothetical: it emits depends_on from
BOTH extractors, 2,310 of them, and the subject qualifier is the only thing keeping 2,304 C# type
dependencies out of the joins. Six verified edges, each a real dependsOn between two real resources.
